headline: A rough day across the board — PLS slammed 8.7% and TTWO dropped 6.3% last night, while the ASX shed 1.8% and the NASDAQ fell 2.5% as markets globally hit the skids.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: Pilbara got hammered today, closing down 8.7% at $2.64. There's no fresh company-specific news, so this looks like broader lithium sector weakness dragging it down. The long-term PnL picture is painful — down over 60% from your entry — and sentiment around lithium and electric vehicles remains soft.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: Take-Two fell 6.3% last night despite strong GTA 6 pre-order momentum (reports suggest pre-orders are approaching 15 million copies). The drop looks like broader tech and NASDAQ weakness pulling it down rather than any company-specific bad news. The GTA 6 launch story is still very much intact.

movers.name: Alphabet (Google)
movers.note: Google dropped 3.85% last night as the NASDAQ sold off broadly. No specific Alphabet news drove the fall — it's the wider market risk-off mood weighing on big tech. The position is now sitting at an 8.5% overall loss, but the long-term AI and advertising thesis hasn't changed.

movers.name: Global X AI ETF
movers.note: GXAI slipped 1.78% today, tracking weakness in global AI and tech stocks. Tokyo markets also extended losses overnight on uncertainty around the AI outlook. The ETF is down 18% overall from your entry — this one is a long-term bet on the AI theme and needs time.

movers.name: DHHF (BetaShares Diversified All Growth ETF)
movers.note: DHHF dipped 1.46% today, mirroring the broad ASX and global market selloff. No specific catalyst — just the tide going out across all markets. You're essentially flat on this holding overall, which is reassuring given the day's volatility.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: VDHG eased 1.36% today in line with the broader ASX and global market weakness. As a diversified fund across multiple asset classes, this kind of move on a down day is expected — nothing to worry about for a long-term holder.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market Shares ETF
movers.note: VTS fell 1.25% today, reflecting the sharp NASDAQ and S&P falls from last night's US session. The US market had a rough night — S&P down 1.9%, NASDAQ down 2.5% — and VTS priced that in at today's ASX open. You're still up 4.8% overall on this one.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: Microsoft edged down 1.12% last night, a relatively modest fall compared to the broader NASDAQ's 2.5% drop. Azure, Copilot and OpenAI remain strong growth pillars. You're up 16.9% overall on this holding — it's your strongest performer.

movers.name: Vanguard Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: VGE slipped 1.14% today, with emerging markets feeling the pinch of a stronger US dollar and risk-off global sentiment. Europe's contradictory China policy (flagged in world news) is another headwind for EM exposure. Down 5.3% overall from your entry.

watch_today.title: PLS.AX: Painful day, but long-term thesis unchanged — hold
watch_today.detail: Pilbara Minerals crashed 8.7% today to $2.64, extending a brutal drawdown — you're now down over 60% from your entry. There's no fresh company-specific bad news today; this is lithium sector sentiment staying ugly. For a long-term investor, selling now locks in a large loss. Unless you believe the lithium story is permanently broken, sit tight. It would take a genuine thesis-breaking event (e.g. Pilbara cutting production, losing major contracts) to justify selling.

watch_today.title: TTWO: Sharp drop despite GTA 6 looking huge — hold
watch_today.detail: Take-Two fell 6.3% last night but GTA 6 pre-orders are reportedly approaching 15 million copies globally. The drop appears to be pure market-wide tech selling rather than anything specific to Take-Two. The GTA 6 launch is still one of the biggest entertainment events in years and the long-term case is very much intact. Hold firm — this is exactly the kind of volatility to ride through for a long-term investor.

watch_today.title: GXAI.AX: AI ETF under pressure — hold but keep watching
watch_today.detail: GXAI dropped 1.78% today and is now down 18% overall from your entry. Global AI stock uncertainty is weighing on the whole sector, with Tokyo markets also extending losses on the same theme. The long-term AI growth story hasn't cracked — the generative AI market is forecast to reach over $1.2 trillion by 2035 — but expect continued choppiness. No reason to sell; hold and let the thesis play out.

watch_today.title: MSFT: Holding up well in a rough market — stay the course
watch_today.detail: Microsoft only fell 1.12% last night while the NASDAQ dropped 2.5% — a sign of relative strength. You're up 16.9% overall on this holding and it remains your best performer. Azure growth and the Copilot AI push continue to underpin the investment case. Nothing to do here except sit back.

watch_today.title: Chalmers budget update: modest cuts flagged — watch for market impact
watch_today.detail: Treasurer Jim Chalmers has flagged spending cuts in the upcoming mid-year budget update but promised 'not too much' — trying to trim without hurting the economy. With inflation still a concern, the RBA is watching closely. Any budget surprise could move ASX rate-sensitive sectors this week. Keep an eye on the update when it drops.

watch_today.title: Broad market selloff: ASX -1.8%, NASDAQ -2.5% — don't panic
watch_today.detail: It was a tough session everywhere today. The ASX 200 lost 161 points (1.79%) and the NASDAQ shed 626 points (2.49%) last night. Your entire portfolio is in the red today, but every holding is a long-term position — single-day selloffs like this are normal and usually recover. No action needed. US markets open tonight around 11:30 PM AEST — worth checking in tomorrow morning.

world.summary: Global markets sold off, Europe-China tensions simmered, Goldman Sachs gave investors a 2027 outlook, and AI regulation debates intensified worldwide.

stories.title: Europe's China Policy 'Fundamentally Contradictory', Says Former Serbian President Vuk Jeremic
stories.why_it_matters: Former Serbian President Vuk Jeremic argues that Europe is trying to be tough on China economically while still depending on Chinese trade and investment — and that this contradiction is making European policy incoherent. For everyday investors, this matters because Europe-China tensions affect global supply chains, particularly in sectors like EVs, solar panels and tech hardware. If Europe can't settle on a consistent China strategy, it creates ongoing uncertainty for companies and markets that span both regions.

stories.title: Goldman Sachs 2027 Economic Outlook: Cautious Optimism for Investors
stories.why_it_matters: Goldman Sachs has published its 2027 economic outlook, with the report drawing significant attention from investors globally. While the full details aren't available here, Goldman's annual outlooks typically set the tone for how big money moves heading into the following year — influencing everything from bond markets to sector allocations. Worth watching for the key calls on US growth, interest rates and emerging markets, all of which directly affect a diversified portfolio like yours.

stories.title: AI Regulation Debate Goes Global: UN, US and Australia All Moving
stories.why_it_matters: Multiple bodies — the United Nations, individual governments, and advocacy groups — are simultaneously pushing for AI regulation, but they can't agree on who should be in charge or what the rules should be. Democracy Without Borders argues that any UN-level AI governance needs genuine democratic input, not just big-power horse-trading. For investors in AI-exposed stocks and ETFs, this regulatory uncertainty is a real risk: heavy-handed rules could slow AI deployment and hit company revenues.

stories.title: GTA 6 Hacker Pleads Guilty Ahead of Sentencing
stories.why_it_matters: The hacker who leaked GTA 6 footage and carried out cyberattacks on Rockstar Games, Uber and Revolut has admitted to the crimes ahead of sentencing. The case highlights serious vulnerabilities in corporate cybersecurity, even at some of the world's largest companies. For Take-Two/Rockstar specifically, the hack caused significant reputational damage in 2022 — the guilty plea closes that legal chapter and removes an overhang for the company.

stories.title: GTA 6 Pre-Orders Approach 15 Million Copies Globally
stories.why_it_matters: GTA 6 pre-orders are reportedly nearing 15 million copies, with total pre-order sales value hitting the equivalent of around NT$48 billion (roughly AUD $2.2 billion). That's a staggering number before the game has even launched. For Take-Two shareholders, this is very good news — it confirms the game is on track to be one of the biggest entertainment launches in history and should translate into massive revenue when it hits shelves.

markets.summary: A broad and bruising session. The ASX 200 fell 1.8% today, tracking the NASDAQ's 2.5% drop from last night's US session. Tech and growth stocks led the selloff. Gold is up slightly as investors seek safety, while the Aussie dollar slipped a little against the USD.

indicators.name: ASX 200
indicators.note: Broad ASX selloff today — financials, materials and tech all dragged lower.

indicators.name: S&P 500
indicators.note: Last night's US session was rough. S&P fell nearly 2% on broad risk-off selling.

indicators.name: NASDAQ Composite
indicators.note: Tech took the brunt of it — NASDAQ dropped 2.5% last night, hurting your US tech holdings.

indicators.name: Crude Oil (WTI)
indicators.note: Oil edged lower — not a dramatic move, more a reflection of softer global growth sentiment.

indicators.name: Gold
indicators.note: Gold nudged higher as investors sought safe havens amid the market selloff. Still near record levels.

indicators.name: AUD/USD
indicators.note: The Aussie dollar slipped slightly, which buffers some of the losses on your US holdings when converted back to AUD.

politics.summary: Jim Chalmers is flagging a cautious budget update — spending cuts are coming but he's promising they won't be aggressive. The RBA released minutes showing internal disagreement on rate hikes, and Labor has reversed course on backpacker work rules.

stories.title: Chalmers Flags Spending Cuts in Mid-Year Budget — 'Not Too Much'
stories.why_it_matters: Treasurer Jim Chalmers says the upcoming Mid-Year Economic and Fiscal Outlook (MYEFO) will include spending cuts, but promises they'll be modest — his exact words were 'cut enough, but not too much.' The juggling act is trying to rein in a budget blowout while not crushing an economy where inflation is still above target. For everyday Aussies, it means some government programs may be trimmed. For markets, a disciplined budget could ease pressure on the RBA to keep rates high for longer.

stories.title: RBA Minutes Reveal Split: Dissenters Warned of 'Materially Sharper Downturn'
stories.why_it_matters: Minutes from the Reserve Bank of Australia's latest meeting show that board members who voted against raising interest rates did so because they were worried a hike could cause a 'materially sharper economic downturn' than necessary. This reveals genuine division inside the RBA — not everyone agrees rates need to stay high. For mortgage holders and investors, this is a hopeful sign that the RBA is at least weighing the downside risks of overtightening before making its next move.

stories.title: Labor Backflips on Backpacker Regional Work Policy
stories.why_it_matters: Labor has reversed a planned policy that would have restricted how long backpackers could work in regional Australia. The original plan was meant to push more Australians into regional jobs, but farming and hospitality industries pushed back hard, warning it would cause labour shortages in rural areas. The backflip means backpackers can continue working in the regions under existing rules — good news for regional employers but a political embarrassment for the government.

stories.title: Albanese Signs AI Supply Chain Pact with Trump at Quad Summit
stories.why_it_matters: Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has signed Australia up to a US-led AI supply chain agreement at the Quad summit (the security grouping of Australia, the US, India and Japan). The deal involves aligning AI chip and hardware supply chains among the four nations — in practice, that means Australia is backing the US approach to keeping advanced AI hardware away from rivals like China. It's a significant geopolitical commitment and ties Australia more closely to the US tech ecosystem, which could have implications for Australian tech policy and trade.

ai.summary: AI regulation is the dominant theme today — Australia, the UN and the US are all wrestling with how to govern AI. Meanwhile, a Stanford-founded AI startup launches with $110M, Apple kicks off an AI health study, and the generative AI market is tipped to hit $1.2 trillion by 2035.

stories.title: Australia to Impose Mandatory AI Safety Rules — But Are We Targeting the Right Risks?
stories.why_it_matters: Australia is moving toward making AI safety rules mandatory rather than voluntary — a significant policy shift. The debate is about which risks to focus on: some experts worry the government is targeting headline-grabbing harms (like deepfakes) while missing subtler but more serious risks like AI bias in hiring or healthcare decisions. For Australian businesses using AI tools, mandatory rules mean compliance costs are coming. For tech investors, it's another sign that the free-for-all phase of AI development is ending globally.

stories.title: Marc Andreessen: AI Regulation Will Protect Jobs — But Kill Economic Growth
stories.why_it_matters: Venture capital legend Marc Andreessen has argued that government regulation of AI will protect some jobs in the short term — but at the cost of slower economic growth and lost competitiveness. He's essentially saying: regulate AI and you'll fall behind countries that don't. This is the central tension in the global AI debate. For investors, Andreessen's view is that over-regulation is a bigger long-term risk than under-regulation — and that the US (and by extension US tech stocks) could suffer if Washington overreaches.

stories.title: Stanford AI Professors Launch Noeri with $110M to Let Companies Own Their Own AI
stories.why_it_matters: A startup called Noeri, founded by leading Stanford AI professors, has launched with $110 million in funding. The company's pitch is that businesses should be able to build and own their own AI models — rather than renting access from OpenAI or Google. That's a direct challenge to the 'AI-as-a-service' model that Big Tech is banking on. If Noeri succeeds, it could reduce corporate dependence on companies like Microsoft (Azure AI) and Google — worth watching for how this plays out.

stories.title: Apple Launches Research Study to Explore AI in Healthcare
stories.why_it_matters: Apple has announced a formal research study to explore how AI can be used in healthcare. The company isn't sharing full details yet, but it signals Apple is moving beyond fitness tracking into genuine medical AI — think AI that could help detect diseases, monitor chronic conditions or personalise treatment. This is a massive potential market, and Apple entering it seriously puts pressure on Google Health and Microsoft's healthcare AI efforts.

stories.title: Generative AI Market Headed for $1.2 Trillion by 2035 as OpenAI, Google and Microsoft Scale Up
stories.why_it_matters: A new market report projects the global generative AI market — covering companies like OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft, Google and NVIDIA — will reach USD $1.206 trillion by 2035. These companies are raising record amounts of capital and scaling revenue rapidly right now. For holders of MSFT, GOOG and AI-focused ETFs like GXAI, this is the core long-term thesis: the market is enormous and still in its early innings. Short-term volatility doesn't change that trajectory.

sport.summary: The NRL Grand Final is done — Roosters pip the Knights 19-18 in a thriller at Accor Stadium. AFL silly season is in full swing with trade week deals and mock drafts flying around.

stories.title: Roosters Beat Knights 19-18 in NRL Grand Final Thriller
stories.why_it_matters: The Sydney Roosters won the 2026 NRL premiership by the narrowest of margins, defeating the Newcastle Knights 19-18 at Accor Stadium on Sunday. One point in a Grand Final — doesn't get more dramatic than that. The Roosters clinch another title in what was a heart-stopping finish for fans of both clubs.

stories.title: Kevin Walters Eyes Fourth NRL Signing as St Helens Circle Long-Term Prospect
stories.why_it_matters: NRL legend Kevin Walters is reportedly pursuing a fourth NRL player for English Super League club St Helens, with a 'long-term prospect' in their sights. Walters, now coaching at St Helens, is building an NRL pipeline into the English competition. No name has been confirmed yet, but it shows the growing crossover between NRL talent and the European rugby league scene.

stories.title: Adelaide Crows in Trade Talks with Victorian Club for Major Draft Pick
stories.why_it_matters: The Adelaide Crows are deep in trade negotiations with an unnamed Victorian AFL club, with a significant draft pick at the centre of the deal. AFL trade period is in full swing and the Crows are clearly looking to move up the draft order. The Victorian club involved hasn't been named, but speculation is rife. If the deal lands a top-10 pick for Adelaide, it could reshape their list-building strategy heading into 2027.

stories.title: SEN Releases 2026 AFL Mock Draft Top 50
stories.why_it_matters: SEN has published its 2026 AFL Mock Draft top 50 prospects ahead of the national draft. The list gives AFL fans a detailed look at who's likely to be snapped up and by whom — key reading for supporters of clubs with early picks. No specific names are available from the article text, but the full ranking is on SEN's website.

stories.title: Canberra-Based AFL Club in 'Tracking Well' Talks with Top-Level Talent
stories.why_it_matters: The Greater Western Sydney Devils are reportedly in talks with a high-profile AFL player, with negotiations described as 'tracking well.' The identity of the player hasn't been confirmed publicly yet, but Canberra-based AFL expansion is a hot topic heading into the 2027 season. A marquee signing could significantly lift the club's profile and fan base in the capital.
